entries.title: The Best Adventure Novels: The 2026 Wilbur Smith Prize, recommended by Alex Bescoby
entries.summary: What makes a great adventure novel? For Alex Bescoby, filmmaker, traveller and judge of the 2026 Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize, it’s the ability to transport readers to unfamiliar worlds and bring history vividly to life. Here, he discusses the six shortlisted novels, from ancient Britain to revolutionary India, exploring stories of endurance, rebellion and remarkable perseverance in the fa
entries.content:
You’re one of the judges of this year’s Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize. Before we get to the books that have been shortlisted, can you tell us a bit about your qualifications as an adventurer?

I’m a professional traveller and filmmaker. I tell stories from faraway places. The projects I do are through a company called Grammar Productions, and what unites them is travel and history—a journey with a pedigree of some sort. I’ve worked across five continents and done all sorts of things, but I guess I’m probably best known for a series called The Last Overland and the book that I wrote about that. It was about a journey from Singapore to London in a 1950s Land Rover. It was recreating a journey from the 1995-6, called the First Overland.

I now run a production company that sends people all over the world doing great journeys with great stories behind them.

And is there always a lot of history involved?

I studied history, and it’s my favourite subject. It gives any journey, in the present day, a greater meaning if you are investigating something that went before, whether that’s following in the footsteps of an author that’s been dead for centuries, or going in search of a lost civilization, or just going to the end of the lane with your daughter. It’s trying to learn something about why the world is the way it is that makes a journey worthwhile.

In terms of the books on the 2026 adventure writing shortlist, what qualities were you looking for when you were deciding which one should be the winner?

I’m a nonfiction travel writer, which is easy because you’re going from A to B.  You maybe have to find a narrative around it, but you’re basically dealing with something that’s happened. Whereas I admire anyone who writes fiction because you’ve got this infinite universe of possibility, and you’ve got to make it work.

The lens I applied when judging was, ‘Does this take me on a journey where I learn about a part of the world or a period of history—or both—that I had no idea about, and do it in a way that didn’t feel like homework?’ If I’m going to dedicate my time to a book, I want to come away having learnt about a place or a person. I love historical fiction or anything that takes its leap from real people and real places. That really inspires me.

My favourite book of all time is The Glass Palace by Amitav Ghosh. It’s the book that started my career. I knew nothing about Southeast Asia. It was a book that was so well written that not only did I leave it feeling like I could enter that world for a bit, I then decided to dedicate my whole academic and professional life to it for about 10 years.

That’s what I’m looking for.

Let’s turn to the books that made the shortlist of the 2026 Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize. First up is The Tarot Reader of Versailles by Anya Bergman. So this is historical fiction with fantastical elements, but based on a true story. Tell me about it and why you liked it.

This is the book I wanted to pick up first, just because I have a soft spot for the French Revolution. The Ancien Régime and the 18th century is just a fascinating period of French history. It’s about a character who I now know was real, but I’d never heard of. I enjoyed the book because the historical setting was something I’d spent a lot of time reading about, but the story was told through the eyes of a character that I didn’t know existed. It was just a really enjoyable romp.

And the main character was a tarot reader?

Yes, you get them today. She was the celebrity shaman of the day. She was reading the fortunes of the great and good in the midst of this time of complete turbulence, and—whether it’s true or not—having an impact on the way that events are unfolding. That mixture of realpolitik and superstition and fortune-telling—I loved it.

Let’s go to the next book, which is set in late Iron Age or early Roman Britain. This is Boudicca’s Daughter by Elodie Harper.

I have a real soft spot for Boudicca. There’s a massive statue of her on Westminster Bridge in London. The Victorians loved Boudicca. She was seen as an ancient British rebel against the Romans, which is weird because she’s from a completely alien culture to what we consider as England from Alfred the Great onwards. She was part of a culture and with a language that we wouldn’t recognise today, but she’s embraced as this national hero.

I also love reading about Dark Age Britain—I’m a huge Bernard Cornwell fan.

The only thing I knew about Boudicca’s daughters was that they were raped. That was the inciting incident for Boudicca’s revolt. They’re never named, and you never hear anything about their story in the sources.

What I really loved about this book is that it brought to life somebody who was just a footnote. It builds a whole world and a life for this person we know nothing about. It’s done in such a way that, as long as you accept that it’s fiction, it was a really good way of trying to step into the shoes of someone who has found themselves on the edge of two worlds.

And is it a realistic kind of depiction of that world, do you think?

I mean, as much as we can be realistic about a culture that was essentially eradicated and happened a very long time ago. There’s not a lot to work from, but I found the story compelling.

Let’s go on to Esperance by Adam Oyebanji. What was this one about?

This was probably the most ambitious book on the shortlist. It’s really unique. It mixed murder mystery, sci-fi and the slave trade. The author is a fascinating man whose day job is exposing financial terrorism and sanctions evasion and investigating high financial crime.

The book starts off with this mad, impossible murder and takes you on this journey. What I loved about it was that it taught me aspects of the history of the slave trade that I wasn’t aware of. So that was very interesting.

Is it set in the present or in the past?

A mix.

Next we have The Fertile Earth by Ruthvika Rao. This was the winner of this year’s Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize—please tell me why it’s such a great book.

I knew it was the winner from the moment I started reading it. It follows a family over time. It’s quite similar to The Glass Palace in that it takes place across several decades in India, although 100 years or so later. It’s set in post-independence India, in the 1960s and 70s, during the Naxalite uprisings around Hyderabad. I’ve read a lot of Southeast Asian history, but I never knew much about the Naxalites. Now I understand who they were and what they were trying to do.

The writing is exquisite, and you wouldn’t need to know or care about India in the 1960s and 70s to find this book unbelievably moving. I’ve worked a lot in India, so when she’s describing the colours and smells—which she does amazingly—I think, ‘I’ve been to places like that. I know what that thing she’s describing smells like. I know what that tree looks like. I know what the dress she’s talking about looks like.’

It sounds amazing.

It’s one of those books that I was literally finishing it at seven in the morning. My daughter woke up and she was crawling all over me, but I just carried on reading to the end.

And what was the Naxalite uprising about? What was the cause of it?

It was a dismantling of the Raj, but also of a system that was much, much older than that—a feudal system where you had the landowners overseeing an indebted, indentured servitude. They had generational farming families and the landowner in the grand house in the middle. It was a form of modern slavery, where families were expected to send workers to the house for free.

It tells the story from both sides. It tells it from the perspective of the landowners, this class of privileged Indians in a world that’s falling apart, but it also tells it from the Naxalite point of view. It shows why people joined this incredibly ruthless, brutal, bloody, murderous campaign to dismantle the feudal system. It’s horrific. It starts off with a horrific mass murder and ends by going back to it again.

The next book takes us to 1920s London. This is Poor Girls by Clare Whitfield.

This one’s great fun. It’s a story about 1920s gang culture, with female protagonists. It’s really well written, and it’s pacy, and the characters are great. The question we asked ourselves as judges is, ‘What counts as an adventure?” This is not the classic Joseph Campbell hero’s journey, necessarily. No one goes on a great adventure and comes back. But there is an adventure here. A woman breaks out of her life and enters a life of crime and has an adventure along the way.

Having spoken to judges of the prize in previous years, my feeling is that the Wilbur Smith Prize is trying to broaden the definition of an adventure.

Yes, my own book The Last Overland is more the standard formula of the hero’s journey—someone feeling the call of adventure, and going out and documenting their own change across six months.

In these books, you’re following a character across time, and it is an adventure. There’s endurance, there’s rebellion, there’s amazing perseverance in the face of hardship. In each of these books, you will find a character that is inspiring—someone who spurs you to go out and see more of the world and do something you didn’t think you could do beforehand.

And last but not least on the shortlist we have White Road, an eco-thriller set on an Arctic oil rig by Harry Whitehead. What’s this one about?

It’s just a cracking murder mystery adventure, and really well written. I actually started out in the oil industry; it was my very first job. I never worked on a rig—and certainly not an Arctic one—but I know the kind of characters in that industry. I know how hard a life it is, and the strange people that it attracts.

It’s a great read. It really transports you into that world. Interestingly, a lady came up to me at the prize event. We were talking about the book, and she said, ‘I’m from the high Canadian Arctic, and I was amazed at how somebody from Scotland had written it so well.’ So that’s not praise coming from me, but from someone from northern Canada, which speaks well of Harry’s research.

I’ve seen it described as part oil rig drama, part survival story. Does that sound right?

Yes, it does. And with a bit of a ghost story in the middle of it as well, which is nice.

Interview by Sophie Roell, Editor

October 18, 2026. Updated: October 20, 2026

entries.title: Biographies for Kids
entries.summary: Biographies are a great way for kids to feel inspired by people who have achieved extraordinary things. And by enabling children to see the world through other people’s eyes, biographies can introduce them to different times and places, helping to broaden their perspectives. Here is a selection of biographies for kids that have been recommended on Five Books. This interview appeared first on Five
entries.content:
Biographies are a great way for kids to feel inspired by people who have achieved extraordinary things. And by enabling children to see the world through other people’s eyes, biographies can introduce them to different times and places, helping to broaden their perspectives. Here is a selection of biographies for kids that have been recommended on Five Books.

Biographies not only introduce kids to inspirational role models, but can teach them important life lessons. Through the stories of real individuals, children learn about the different values that drive people, and that success is usually preceded by obstacles and setbacks. Biographies can also be a good way to teach empathy and self-awareness, as young readers get glimpses of lives that are very different from their own.

Picture books for young readers that have been recommended on Five Books include gorgeous biographies of 13th century poet and scholar Rumi, and contemporary musician Evelyn Glennie.

If you are after longer picture books (over 40 pages) for slightly older readers, recommendations include Voice of Freedom about Civil Rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer, The People’s Painter about the life and work of Benjamin Shahn, I Dissent about US Supreme Court justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, and The Fire of Stars, which is a brilliant combination of biography for children about astrophysicist Cecilia Payne and the birth of a star.

Josephine: A Dazzling Life is about the extraordinary life of 20th century icon Josephine Baker. It is a longer book at around a hundred pages, and is an easy, fully illustrated read to fascinate children and adults alike.

Publisher Barrington Stoke specialises in dyslexia-friendly books designed to be both interesting, quick reads for confident readers as well as accessible stories for those who find reading more challenging. That includes some excellent biographical fiction for kids, such as Journey Back to Freedom about the early life of Olaudah Equiano, Elisabeth and the Box of Colours about Élisabeth Louise Vigée Le Brun (said to be Queen Marie Antoinette’s favourite portrait artist), and Respect! about the Black English professional footballer and World War 1 British army officer Walter Tull.

Continuing with recommendations for the 8-12 age range, librarian Alison King recommends the multi award-winning graphic novel The Bird in Me Flies, inspired by the life of Swedish artist Berta Hansson.

Finally, another biography with amazing artwork is the story of 17th century scientist Maria Sibylla Merian; this is surely one of the most beautifully illustrated biographies for kids ever, featuring as it does her own nature drawings.

October 18, 2026

entries.title: The Best Novels of 2026: The Booker Prize Shortlist, recommended by Rebecca Liu
entries.summary: Each year, judges for the Booker Prize whittle their longlist down to a five- or six-book shortlist for the title of the best new novel of the previous twelve months. This year, the finalists include two previous Booker winners– Douglas Stuart and Marlon James – and a previous shortlistee in Elizabeth Strout. We asked Rebecca Liu, 2026 judge and Guardian journalist, to talk us through the shortlis
entries.content:
Thanks for agreeing to talk to us about the 2026 Booker Prize shortlist. It’s an exciting shortlist—all books I’ve either already read and admired or am excited to read. What were you looking for, when you were looking for the best novels of the year?

It’s my pleasure. I didn’t go into the process with specific criteria in mind, though, over time, I found myself drawn to novels with rich and interesting sentences, which made surprising and risky choices and opened a hidden window on the world. In her memoir Priestdaddy, Patricia Lockwood – also a judge this year – has a lovely line about what good books can do: to give you a feeling that “life can be holdable in the hand, examined down to the dog hairs, eaten with the eyes and understood.” That rang true for me.

The first book on the 2026 Booker Prize shortlist is M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything, which features a beachcomber who discovers a very strange object. Perhaps you’d tell us more – and why the judges admire it.

This mysterious, haunting novel is set in post-apocalyptic Britain after an alien invasion, where no-one knows what’s going on. It’s full of intriguing, counter-intuitive turns of phrase that upend our usual understanding of language – the sea is described as turning “into speech”; dawn is an “exotic form of sunset, some vast, gorgeous, fragile glitch in the real” – and captures a general sense of confusion and loss, a deep melancholia and uncertainty about a viable future, that feels very true to contemporary England.

M. John Harrison is often described as “genre-defying” – would you expand on that, why you think that is?

This is a beautifully weird novel with markers of science fiction – there’s an alien invasion, a strange species that washes up from the sea, and a dystopian future replete with mad scientists – but isn’t too concerned with the exposition or world-building as we might expect. It drops the reader right into the world, and makes them feel that same sense of existential loss as its characters; you too are in that strange haze, trying to work out where you are and why you are here. Violent acts happen and we don’t know why; people make decisions based on inarticulable reasoning – much like they do life. At times the novel almost feels, with its interest in the evocative and atmospheric and associational language, like poetry.

Next on the 2026 Booker Prize shortlist is Marlon James’s The Disappearers. Would you introduce it to our readers?

This bold and challenging novel confronts homophobia in 1980s Jamaica by following a group of gay men who decide to stage a play about queer life in Kingston. It’s formally wide-ranging, with sections composed of letters, reported speech, and diary entries, and the story itself contains so much heart and so much violence. There are sentences in that book that made me belly-laugh; other times a scene would be so confronting in its brutality that I had to put the book down, go into a dark room and stare into the void for twenty minutes. At 640 pages, it’s the longest book on the shortlist, and that kind of maximalist attitude seeps into everything about the book: from its language, its experimentalism, its prose, its swagger and fury.

Marlon James won the 2015 Booker Prize with A Brief History of Seven Killings. Do you take into account an author’s previous work or achievements while judging? In some cases, it must be difficult not to at least bear it in mind.

We’re not supposed to consider any of that, and just focus on the novel itself. Book world chatter does happen around you, of course, though I found ways to artificially isolate myself from it. When I was reading, my commitment to the purity of the text extended so far as to avoid reading blurbs, supportive quotes, biographies and author photos – I covered some with post-it notes.

Maybe that brings me to our next book, John of John, also by a previous Booker Prize winner; Douglas Stuart won it in 2020. It centres on a strict island community on Harris, in Scotland’s Outer Hebrides. Would you talk us through the book and why it is notable?

A difficult relationship between a father and son forms the heart of this book: Cal is a graduate who has returned home after fashion school, and his father John is a repressed, lonely man with secrets of his own. Set in the nineties, this lovely novel evokes a rich sense of time and place, drawing out the social world of the island of Harris.

Two phrases come to mind when I think about this book. First, ‘texture’: the novel deftly weaves in many beautiful details and builds such a vivid, granular sense of its world and its characters. It’s as though you could reach your hand right into the pages and feel the grit of Harris. Second, ‘slow burn’: the novel has a way of building these little details into something wonderful.

Next we have The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout, a previous shortlistee, which follows a history teacher who wrestles with a deep sense of loneliness. Would you tell us more?

How do you write about contemporary American politics without reproducing the mania and fear that makes things feel so violently hopeless and deranged? This is a wise and poignant novel that explores what happens to the individual psyche during times of visible cruelty and mistrust. Artie Dam is a history teacher living in Massachusetts who has lived thus far with an innate and uncomplicated sense of goodness, but as the world shifts around him, he grows more used to cynicism and dishonesty. Strout writes about this slow corruption with such precision and grace; it’s both heartfelt and deeply sad.

Speaking more generally, there are sometimes, understandable, questions about the relevance of the novel in unstable and violent times – is it just a navel-gazing toothless art form, et cetera. I often think about what the author Elif Batuman once wrote in response: that great writers have always illustrated compelling interiority in times of social upheaval, and when these stories succeed, show the importance of people having a right to their own private dramas.

I think this is very much a novel that speaks to that point, and also links the two spheres of the public and private: it shows what is happening out there in politics not only affects our social and economic worlds, but also in the – allow me to be very uncool and sentimental here – matters of the soul.

I think that brings us to Luke Kennard’s Black Bag, which portrays a social experiment in which an actor is hired to sit through a term of lectures inside a leather sack. It’s inspired by real events at Oregon University, I believe. Quite different in tone to the Strout – but the judges admired it?

Reading 163 books in seven months really makes you appreciate the wide range of novels being published at the moment. It showed us that there are many ways to write a great novel, and we wanted our longlist and shortlist to reflect that. We also found that writing good comedy is very difficult. Black Bag is a funny and clever book about a struggling actor in modern-day Britain, who in his desperation takes up this strange job, which takes him to even stranger places. The novel touches on several zeitgeisty themes – the difficulty of being an artist today without inherited wealth, why men are having a weird time – with a warm intelligence and lightness of touch.

Kennard is an award-winning poet. Does that come through in his prose?

The novel has so many sharp, memorable sentences that capture our moment of collective derangement and debasement. Here are some I underlined:

He closes his laptop: the contemporary moment’s gesture of generosity nonpareil.

Stockbrokers are described as:

a priestly caste in the later days of a once great civilisation, guardians of arcane spell books, fat on their banquets and delirious on their own perfumes, bereft of any sense of duty or responsibility. No love.

And:

We lay claim to a form of sexual liberation, says Claudio, but the attendant humiliation literally kills people.

to which our narrator responds

Sex is really weird, that’s for sure.

I’m not a poet myself, though judges Raymond Antrobus and Patricia Lockwood taught me so much about reading with a poet’s eye and ear. There is so much personality, humour and wisdom in these sentences; they also contain a nice rhythm and an understanding of human life that makes you want to both laugh and throw the book across the room in cringing, despairing recognition. So, to answer your original question: possibly, yes!

The same might also apply to poet-turned-novelist Rebecca Perry, who is our final shortlistee with May We Feed the King. Tell us more.

We admired the beauty of its prose, its artful and wonderfully strange story, and how it thoughtfully engages with questions of power, legacy and history. A historical curator in modern-day Britain is commissioned by a former palace to recreate past scenes of glory; we then jump back in time to life at a medieval court, in which a reluctant king ascends the throne. There’s so much here about the nature of power and ambition, and how the historical narratives we often receive without question today are shaped. With this book, I think about that quality of ‘aliveness’: much like how the curator herself prizes staging historical scenes infused with a sense of life, as though her subjects had just moments before left the room, we were impressed by just how immersive and vivid and richly observed the story in the medieval court felt. You can really feel the claustrophobia, the judgment and the swirling ambitions of the court as you read.

How did you find the judging process—and has it changed how you read and understand fiction, would you say?

It’s been hugely pleasurable and so much fun, and has brought me back to the best parts of university, when life was just about reading rich, interesting texts and discussing them with clever and passionate people. I’m already trying to start new book clubs to pre-emptively fill the sad gaping hole in my life that will open up once this is over. It has made me appreciate good writing and good editing, and perhaps – speaking as a sometimes critic – even slightly broken criticism for me.

Reading all these books shows how difficult it is to write a well-executed novel, to the point where I’ve sometimes wondered about the point of further contestations about things like pose and theme and affect about what are basically and fundamentally well-written books. But we must plough on, because it is worth thinking through, albeit with more generosity in my own heart.

What will you be thinking about when you decide on the winning novel?

I went to a talk by Ben Okri recently, who said there were two types of novels: first, the ‘private garden’ books, ie the kinds of texts that derive from the particular imagination and interiority of the author, and are often perhaps more weird, jagged and mysterious as a result; and second, the ‘in the world’ books that pick up on and respond to things in our external world – politics, social movements, et cetera.

It got me thinking about how, on occasion, you’ll encounter a book that through some mysterious and gorgeous alchemy is about to do both in its own idiosyncratic way. Perhaps that is what makes a future classic. Bring on November!

 

The winner of the 2026 Booker Prize will be announced on Monday, 9 November. 

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor
